name: Blue light acne device

angle.text: Users apply blue light devices to acne-prone skin to cut inflammatory breakouts. Clinic-strength blue light has been studied for mild to moderate acne; evidence for lower-powered home devices is thinner.

summary: Reduces some inflammatory acne lesions.
currentQuick:
A blue light acne device is a handheld wand or mask that emits visible blue light, around 405 to 470 nanometers, onto acne-prone skin for a few minutes a day. Dermatology clinics use stronger versions, and consumer devices are lower power.
It is used as a drug-free adjunct for mild to moderate inflammatory acne.
How it works: Cutibacterium acnes produces porphyrins that absorb blue light and generate reactive oxygen species, damaging the bacteria. The light may also have a mild anti-inflammatory effect on the skin.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are minor, such as temporary dryness or redness, and eye protection is advised. Meta-analyses find blue light can reduce lesions, but included trials are small, short and at risk of bias, so effectiveness versus standard treatments remains unclear. Combination blue and red light may do better in the short term, and home devices are weaker than clinic units.
deepLead:
A blue light acne device is a handheld wand, mask or panel that emits visible blue light, typically in the 405 to 470 nanometre range, onto acne-prone skin for several minutes per session. Clinics use higher-powered units, while consumer devices are lower in power.
Blue light is used as a drug-free option for mild to moderate inflammatory acne. Its proposed mechanism is that Cutibacterium acnes produces porphyrins that absorb blue light and generate reactive oxygen species that damage the bacterium, and that the light may also have mild anti-inflammatory effects.
A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Annals of Family Medicine, a 2021 systematic review, and a Cochrane-based review of light therapies for acne have examined the trials. Reviewers describe the studies as generally small, short and at risk of bias, so effectiveness relative to standard treatments is uncertain. Home devices are weaker than clinic units.

name: At-home fractional laser

angle.text: Users try low-energy handheld fractional lasers for fine lines, texture, mild scars and uneven tone. Clinic fractional lasers are well studied; evidence for home versions is more limited and varies by device.

summary: Fine lines and texture; the strongest home-device category in the 2026 review — device-dependent.
currentQuick:
At-home fractional lasers are low-energy, non-ablative handheld devices that treat the skin in a grid of tiny microscopic zones rather than the whole surface. They are sold for fine lines, uneven texture and mild scarring on the face.
They are a consumer version of professional fractional resurfacing and are positioned as one of the stronger device categories for home use, though far gentler than clinic treatments.
How it works: The laser creates microscopic thermal injury columns in the epidermis and dermis, surrounded by untouched skin, which triggers wound healing and new collagen production. Home devices deliver much lower energy, so changes accumulate gradually over repeated sessions.
Risks and caveats: Possible effects include redness, dryness, temporary pigment change and, with misuse, burns or infection; sun protection and skin-type suitability matter. Reviews of home devices rank fractional lasers, LED and radiofrequency as having the best efficacy-safety balance, but no systematic review focused only on home fractional lasers was found and quality of evidence varies by device. Results are modest compared with clinic procedures.
deepLead:
An at-home fractional laser is a handheld, low-energy, typically non-ablative device that delivers light to the skin in a grid of tiny zones, leaving surrounding tissue untouched. Consumer versions are sold for fine lines, uneven texture and mild scarring on the face, and are lower-powered relatives of clinic fractional resurfacing.
The clinic technology has a substantial literature. Fractional photothermolysis with a 1,550 nm erbium fibre laser was studied for atrophic scars in 2007, a consensus report addressed ablative fractional resurfacing for traumatic scars in 2014, and systematic reviews have examined fractional CO2 lasers for depressed acne scars. Home devices have a much thinner evidence base.
A 2026 review of home-based dermatologic devices for acne and rejuvenation and a 2022 systematic review of home-based dermatology devices are the main overviews; the latter included 37 studies of 16 devices, and found no double-blinded randomized trials among them. The 2022 review's laser findings concerned hair growth in androgenic alopecia and not fractional skin resurfacing.

name: RF skin-tightening device

angle.text: Users use home radiofrequency devices to firm skin and sharpen the jaw and neck contour. Clinic RF is studied for modest tightening; evidence for lower-power home devices is more limited.

summary: Modest, real tightening with consistent use.
currentQuick:
A home radiofrequency skin-tightening device uses low-power radio waves delivered through metal electrodes pressed against the face to warm the skin. It is sold for wrinkles, lax skin and a firmer facial contour.
It is a lower-power relative of clinic radiofrequency treatments and is one of the home devices with published randomized data.
How it works: Radiofrequency energy heats the dermis, which shrinks existing collagen fibers and prompts fibroblasts to produce new collagen over weeks. Consistent use is needed because each session delivers only mild heating.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are mild redness and warmth, with burns possible from overheating or poor contact. Small randomized and open-label trials show modest wrinkle improvement, but wrinkle scores decline again after use stops, and many studies are short and sponsor-linked. Reported results are subtle tightening rather than the effect of a surgical facelift.
deepLead:
A home radiofrequency (RF) skin-tightening device is a handheld or wearable unit that passes low-power radio-frequency energy into the skin through metal electrodes to warm the dermis. It is sold for fine lines, skin laxity and a firmer facial contour, and is a lower-power relative of clinic RF treatments.
Wikipedia describes RF skin tightening as a technique that heats skin to stimulate collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production, offering an alternative to facelift surgery; it states that a dermal temperature of about 67 degrees Celsius has been reported as ideal for remodelling in clinic treatments. Clinic monopolar RF (the ThermaCool system) was described in a 2007 review as supported by published evidence for mild to moderate facial laxity and wrinkles.
Home devices have a smaller evidence base. A 2022 randomized split-face trial of a home RF and red-LED device found improvements versus a cosmetic comparator over 12 weeks, but was small, unblinded to participants and manufacturer-supported. A 2022 systematic review of home-based dermatology devices graded RF for wrinkles as supported by one randomized trial and six lower-level studies and noted the lack of long-term data.

name: Microcurrent device

angle.text: Users apply microcurrent as a non-invasive facelift, often before events, for a lifted look and less puffiness. Small studies suggest short-lived effects; claims about masseter pain, ATP or anxiety treatment are weakly supported.

summary: The "lifted" look is real — and gone by tomorrow.
currentQuick:
Microcurrent devices pass very low electrical current, in the microampere range, into the face through metal or gel-coated probes. They are sold as a non-invasive facelift that tones the muscles and lifts the contour.
An instantly tighter look is commonly reported, and the devices are popular as a pre-event routine.
How it works: The current is claimed to mimic the body's own electrical signals, stimulating facial muscles and cellular energy production. The visible lifting is thought to come from temporary muscle activation and fluid shifts rather than structural change in skin.
Risks and caveats: The devices are generally well tolerated, with tingling or mild redness; they are not suitable for people with pacemakers or certain implants or during pregnancy. Evidence is limited: a review notes few studies specific to home microcurrent devices, and the only randomized trial found was of a neuromuscular stimulation device. Effects are short-lived without continued use.
deepLead:
A microcurrent device passes very low-level electrical current, in the microampere range, into the skin through metal or gel-coated probes. Consumer versions are sold as non-invasive 'facelifts' intended to tone facial muscles and lift the facial contour, and are popular as pre-event routines.
Microcurrent is described in a 2024 evaluation of home beauty devices as using low- to medium-frequency pulsed currents to tighten skin, reduce wrinkles and improve contour. The same authors note that few studies focus on home microcurrent products specifically. In a 2022 systematic review of 37 home dermatology studies, microcurrent did not form a category of its own.
Clinical microcurrent has been studied for other purposes, including pain in masticatory muscles, pressure ulcers and wound healing.

name: Multi-head facial tool

angle.text: Users buy all-in-one facial devices to combine light, microcurrent and massage for fine lines and puffiness. The LED component has more supporting data than the microcurrent head, and trials of the combined devices are limited.

summary: TheraFace-type all-in-ones: the LED head has data, the microcurrent head mostly has marketing.
currentQuick:
Multi-head facial tools, of which TheraFace-type devices are an example, combine interchangeable attachments in one handset, typically LED light, microcurrent, percussive massage, cleansing and cold or heat heads.
They are sold as an all-in-one skincare routine and appeal to users who want several modalities without separate gadgets.
How it works: Each head works by a different mechanism: LED photobiomodulation for collagen and inflammation, microcurrent for muscle stimulation, percussion and temperature for circulation and puffiness. The benefit depends on which heads have supporting evidence.
Risks and caveats: Light-based heads have randomized, sham-controlled data for wrinkle and elasticity gains, but the microcurrent and massage heads have little independent evidence, and most multi-function devices are tested as a package or alongside serums. Costs are high and reported results modest. The same cautions apply as for each mode, including eye and pacemaker precautions.
deepLead:
A multi-head facial tool is a single handheld skincare device sold with interchangeable attachments, each delivering a different type of treatment. Typical heads described in product categories of this kind include LED light, microcurrent, percussive massage, cleansing, and cold or heat applicators. TheraFace-type devices are commonly cited as examples of the format. The devices are marketed as an all-in-one alternative to owning several separate gadgets.
Because each head works by a different mechanism, the evidence behind a multi-head tool is not a single body of evidence. Low-level red and near-infrared light has been studied in randomized, sham-controlled trials of home-use LED devices for wrinkles and skin quality , while facial neuromuscular electrical stimulation has been examined in at least one randomized trial . Published research on the combined handsets themselves is limited to small studies such as a single-patient split-face case report .
Reviews and encyclopedic summaries note that home light devices are generally lower in power than in-office equipment and that evidence for anti-aging effects of red light therapy remains limited . Prices for all-in-one handsets are listed in the site's catalogue at about $420.

name: Sonic cleansing brush

chain: Deeper removal of oil and debris
angle.text: Users cleanse with sonic brushes to remove makeup and sebum more thoroughly than hands, aiming for clearer, brighter skin and fewer breakouts. Studies suggest better debris removal; acne and scar effects are less studied.

summary: Better debris and makeup removal than hands.
currentQuick:
A sonic cleansing brush is a handheld device with a soft bristle head that oscillates at high frequency while cleansing the face. Clarisonic popularized the category, and many brands now sell similar tools.
It is used for deeper removal of makeup, oil and pollution than hands alone and for a smoother-feeling surface.
How it works: The head vibrates thousands of times per minute, loosening debris and sebum from pores and the skin surface, which makes cleansers work more effectively than manual washing.
Risks and caveats: Overuse or rough settings can irritate or over-exfoliate skin, especially for sensitive or acne-prone skin, and bristle heads need replacing to avoid bacterial build-up. Evidence is modest: a clinician review and small studies show better particulate removal and acne improvement in uncontrolled cohorts, but few randomized trials. The documented effect is cleansing rather than anti-aging.
deepLead:
A sonic cleansing brush is a handheld, battery-powered device with a soft-bristled head that oscillates rapidly to cleanse the face. It is used alongside a liquid or gel cleanser, with the stated aim of removing makeup, sebum and environmental particles more thoroughly than washing by hand. Clarisonic is commonly named as the brand that popularised the category, and many manufacturers now sell similar tools.
The published evidence is modest and mostly concerns cleansing rather than anti-aging. A literature review of facial cleansing with sonic brushes has been published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology , a laboratory-style study used an artificial sebum-and-particulate pollution model to compare a sonic brush with manual cleansing , and a multi-center cohort study examined a brush with an acne-specific head and gel cleanser in people with mild-to-moderate acne . No randomized trial is included among these.

name: Dermaplaning razor

chain: Blade removes dead cells and peach fuzz
angle.text: Users shave the face with a single blade to remove peach fuzz and dead skin for an instant smoother, brighter look. Evidence is mostly clinical and anecdotal; improved product absorption and scar benefits are less studied.

summary: Instant peach-fuzz removal and smoother makeup/skin surface.
currentQuick:
Dermaplaning is a form of mechanical exfoliation in which a single sharp blade is drawn lightly across the face to remove the top layer of dead skin cells and fine vellus hair, or peach fuzz. Home versions use small, single-blade facial razors, while professionals use a scalpel.
It is used to get a smoother skin surface, brighter look and more even makeup and skincare application.
How it works: The blade, held at a shallow angle, shaves off the stratum corneum and vellus hair at skin level. The hair follicle is untouched, so hair regrows on its normal schedule, and exfoliation lets products absorb more easily.
Risks and caveats: Risks include nicks, irritation and breakouts, and it is not advised over active acne or inflamed skin. Hair does not grow back thicker or darker, but the effects last only a few weeks. No controlled trials were identified, and the evidence comes from clinic and aesthetics sources, though the mechanism is physically straightforward. Using a clean blade is advised to reduce infection risk.
deepLead:
Dermaplaning is a form of mechanical exfoliation in which a single sharp blade is drawn at a shallow angle across the face to remove the outermost layer of dead skin cells and fine vellus hair, commonly called peach fuzz. Clinicians and aestheticians perform it with a sterile surgical-style blade, and consumer versions are small single-blade facial razors sold for home use, typically at around $10 to $20 .
Users and practitioners describe the purpose as a smoother, brighter-looking skin surface and a more even base for makeup and skincare products. Reported effects last on the order of weeks, since the skin and hair regrow .
Published evidence is limited. A 2011 systematic review of dermaplaning, topical oxygen and light therapy found that the data supporting these noninvasive facial rejuvenation methods were scarce and largely anecdotal . Laboratory studies show that dermaplaning removes part of the stratum corneum and can alter how drugs permeate excised skin , and older surgical literature describes the use of dermatome-based dermaplaning for acne scarring . No controlled trial of the home facial razor for cosmetic smoothing is known.

name: Derma roller (home)

angle.text: Users roll the face with fine needles to soften acne scars and texture and fine lines, and some try it on brows. Professional microneedling has trial data; home rollers use shorter needles with weaker evidence, and infection risk is debated.

summary: Professional microneedling has real collagen data. Home rolling is weak — plus an infection risk.
note: The 2026 device review called home microneedling out specifically.
currentQuick:
A home derma roller is a handheld roller covered in tiny needles, usually 0.25 to 0.5 millimeters at home, rolled across the skin to create microscopic punctures. It is a consumer version of professional microneedling.
It is promoted for scars, texture, fine lines and better absorption of serums.
How it works: Needle punctures trigger a wound-healing response that increases collagen and elastin production in the dermis. Professional devices use longer needles to reach deeper layers, while shorter home needles are reported to produce less effect.
Risks and caveats: Home use carries a risk of infection, irritation, post-inflammatory pigmentation and scarring if the roller is not sterilized or technique is poor. Reviews note that proper sterilization is essential for home rollers. The collagen evidence is for professional microneedling, not home rolling, and no systematic review of home rollers specifically was found.
deepLead:
A home derma roller is a handheld device with a rolling drum or wheel covered in very fine needles, which is rolled across the skin to create many tiny punctures. It is a consumer version of the clinical procedure known as microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, dermarolling or skin needling . Home rollers are generally sold with shorter needles than those used in clinics, commonly in the range of about 0.25 to 0.5 mm, at prices of roughly $10 to $30.
Users and marketers describe it as a tool for scars, texture, fine lines and for improving how skincare serums are absorbed. The proposed mechanism is that micro-injuries trigger a wound-healing response and release of growth factors, leading to collagen production .
Published research is largely about professional microneedling. Reviews of clinic-performed microneedling report improvements for scars, striae, wrinkles, acne scars, melasma, photodamage and some forms of hair loss, with transient redness and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation the more commonly reported adverse events . How much of that evidence applies to shorter-needle devices used at home without clinical sterility has not been established in the sources reviewed here, and no systematic review specific to home rollers was identified.

name: Gua sha stone

angle.text: Users stroke gua sha stones across the face to de-puff and sculpt the jaw and cheeks, and some hope for fewer wrinkles. Evidence for lasting facial change is limited; the effect is generally described as temporary fluid movement.

summary: Massage and transient fluid movement. Pleasant; fleeting.
currentQuick:
Gua sha is a traditional East Asian technique in which a smooth-edged tool, often of jade or rose quartz, is drawn over lubricated skin. A gentler facial version is used in skincare for sculpting and de-puffing.
It is popular on social media as a lymphatic massage and facial contouring step.
How it works: The pressure and stroking motion transiently increase local blood flow and move fluid, which can reduce puffiness for a time. No evidence of lasting structural changes to fat or bone has been reported.
Risks and caveats: Facial use is low risk, though pressing too hard can bruise, and traditional body scraping intentionally raises red marks. The evidence concerns pain relief in the body, which is of low quality, and cosmetic claims for the face have not been substantiated. Results are temporary.
deepLead:
Gua sha is a traditional East Asian technique in which a smooth-edged tool is pressed and stroked over lubricated skin. In its traditional form, applied to the body for pain, colds and fatigue, it is performed until red or purple petechiae, known as sha, appear . A gentler facial version, using stones such as jade or rose quartz, has become popular in skincare, where it is promoted for contouring, de-puffing and lymphatic drainage .
The facial and traditional uses have different evidence bases. Trials of body gua sha have mostly examined pain conditions such as neck and low back pain, and a 2018 meta-analysis of gua sha trials in perimenopausal syndrome found most to be of low methodological quality . Research on cosmetic facial use is sparse: a 2025 randomized trial in 34 women compared facial roller and gua sha massage over 8 weeks on facial contour, muscle tone and skin elasticity , and a 2023 dermatology letter discussed whether gua sha, jade rollers and facial massage offer benefits .
Wikipedia characterises traditional gua sha as a pseudoscientific practice that lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit and notes that it nearly always causes minor skin trauma . Practitioners and traditional medicine texts describe it as releasing stagnation of qi and blood . Facial stones are sold at roughly $10 to $25.

name: Ice roller

angle.text: Users roll a chilled head over the face in the morning to cut puffiness and calm skin before events. Cold's short-term de-puffing effect is plausible; lasting benefits for texture or wrinkles are untested.

summary: Real short-term depuff. Morning-of-event tool.
currentQuick:
An ice roller is a handheld roller with a chilled head, either a frozen gel or a metal cylinder, that is rolled over the face. It is used in short sessions to reduce morning puffiness and calm skin.
It is mainly used the morning of an event for a fresher, less swollen look.
How it works: Cold causes local vasoconstriction, reducing blood flow and fluid leakage into tissue, which lessens puffiness and redness for a short time. The effect fades as the skin rewarms.
Risks and caveats: Risks are minimal if skin is not frozen for long; direct prolonged contact is advised against, and people with cold urticaria, Raynaud's or sensitivity to cold should be cautious. No trial of cold rollers on everyday facial puffiness was identified; the closest evidence is on cold-induced vasoconstriction and post-surgical swelling, so the benefit is considered plausible but short-lived.
deepLead:
An ice roller is a handheld roller with a chilled head, usually a frozen gel-filled or metal cylinder, that is rolled over the face for a short time. It is sold as a skincare tool to reduce morning puffiness and calm the look of skin and is typically priced at about $10 to $20.
The proposed mechanism is that cold causes local vasoconstriction, narrowing blood vessels and limiting fluid leakage into the tissue for a short period. Laboratory work on cutaneous cooling has described a persistent reduction in blood perfusion after cooling , and cold application has been studied as a way of managing swelling after facial surgery . No published trial of a cold roller for everyday facial puffiness was found. The effect is generally described as lasting only until the skin rewarms.

name: Pimple patches

chain: Flatter spot, less scarring and redness
angle.text: Users stick hydrocolloid patches on individual pimples to flatten whiteheads and stop themselves picking, which is meant to mean a less visible blemish and fewer marks afterward. Medicated and microneedle versions are also sold. The absorbing and anti-picking role is widely described, while evidence for the added ingredients is thinner.

summary: Hydrocolloid protects the spot, absorbs drainage, stops you picking.
currentQuick:
Pimple patches are small adhesive stickers, usually hydrocolloid, placed over a blemish for several hours or overnight. Some also contain salicylic acid or microneedles.
They are used to flatten whiteheads and protect spots from picking.
How it works: The hydrocolloid layer absorbs fluid and pus from the lesion and holds a moist, protected environment that supports healing. The patch also acts as a physical barrier that discourages touching and bacterial contamination.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are rare, mainly adhesive irritation or allergy, and they are not effective for deep cystic acne. Evidence is limited: a narrative review says hydrocolloids are studied mostly for wounds with few acne studies, and the one randomized trial found compared two patches rather than with no treatment. They are described as a plausible low-risk aid for individual spots rather than a treatment for acne.
deepLead:
Pimple patches are small adhesive stickers, usually made of hydrocolloid, that are placed over an individual blemish for several hours or overnight. Some versions add salicylic acid or tiny microneedles. They are sold at roughly $5 to $15 per pack and are used to flatten whiteheads and to protect spots from picking.
Hydrocolloid technology originated in wound care. Hydrocolloid dressings combine gel-forming materials such as carboxymethylcellulose, pectin and gelatin with a semipermeable backing, absorbing fluid from a wound and keeping a moist environment . A 2025 narrative review examines the use of hydrocolloids in dermatology, and the evidence specific to acne patches is thin: the identified randomized study compared two types of patch against each other and not against no treatment .

name: Silicone scar sheets

angle.text: People wear silicone sheets over healed scars, including post-acne and surgical ones, to make raised scars flatter and less visible. They are used mainly for hypertrophic scars and keloids. Studies exist for raised scars; their use on typical acne scarring is less studied.

summary: Genuinely improves some raised scars with consistent wear.
currentQuick:
Silicone scar sheets are adhesive, reusable sheets of medical-grade silicone applied over a healed scar for most of the day for weeks to months. They are used for raised hypertrophic scars and keloids, and are sometimes applied after surgery or acne.
They are a standard first-line, non-invasive option and an inexpensive way to treat a visible scar.
How it works: Silicone hydrates the outer skin layer and is thought to regulate fibroblast activity and collagen production through occlusion and gentle pressure, softening and flattening the scar.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are rash, itching or maceration, and sheets must be kept clean. Cochrane reviews describe the evidence as limited and low to very low certainty, with trials of poor quality, though some show improved thickness and color. Reported benefits are modest, and consistent wear is required.
deepLead:
Silicone scar sheets are adhesive, reusable sheets of medical-grade silicone gel that are worn over a healed scar for much of the day over weeks to months. They are used mainly for raised hypertrophic scars and keloids and are sometimes applied after surgery or acne. Consumer packs are typically priced at about $10 to $30.
Silicone gel sheeting has been used in scar management for several decades, and a controlled trial published in 1989 reported its effects on hypertrophic scars . An international panel of experts in 2002 identified silicone gel sheeting and intralesional corticosteroids as having a primary role in managing abnormal scars . A 2010 review concluded that there was good evidence for silicone sheets, pulsed dye laser, intralesional triamcinolone and dermabrasion in reducing hypertrophic scars, with qualifications about timing and scar type . Cochrane reviews of silicone gel sheeting, in contrast, describe the certainty of the evidence as limited because of the quality of trials . Randomized trials have also reported results of no benefit in some settings, such as scar prevention in children with cancer .

name: Under-eye cooling mask

angle.text: Users place cold gel patches under the eyes after sleep or a late night to reduce morning puffiness and tired-looking eyes. It is a form of cryotherapy, mostly studied for injuries and swelling elsewhere. Evidence for puffy eyes specifically is largely anecdotal, and the effect is described as temporary.

summary: Temporarily shrinks morning puffiness.
currentQuick:
An under-eye cooling mask is a reusable gel or cold-pack patch worn over the lower eyelids and cheeks for a few minutes. It is used to reduce puffy eyes after sleep or a late night.
It is a quick, low-cost morning routine for a more rested look.
How it works: Cooling causes vasoconstriction and reduces fluid accumulation in the loose periorbital tissue, easing swelling and redness temporarily.
Risks and caveats: Risks are very low, with rare cold urticaria or skin irritation. Evidence comes from post-surgery swelling studies, where cold gel masks outperformed ice gloves, and not from everyday puffiness, so benefits are considered plausible and short-lived. Persistent bags or swelling can reflect fat, allergy or medical causes that cooling does not address.
deepLead:
An under-eye cooling mask is a reusable gel or cold-pack patch worn over the lower eyelids and cheeks for a few minutes, typically after sleep or a late night, with the aim of reducing the look of puffy eyes. It is a form of local cryotherapy, the therapeutic use of low temperatures, which is more widely used for sprains, muscle soreness and swelling after surgery or soft tissue injury.
The proposed mechanism is that cooling narrows blood vessels and reduces blood flow to swollen tissue. No published trial appears to have tested cooling masks for everyday morning puffiness in otherwise healthy people. The closest evidence comes from surgical patients: a 2024 randomized trial after rhinoplasty found that a cooling gel eye mask was associated with lower pain and swelling scores than ice in a latex glove, and a 2025 pilot study found that a cooled periocular mask reduced eyelid swelling for the first day or so after blepharoplasty.
Cold exposure has documented limits and risks, including contraindications in people with cold allergy or cold-induced urticaria, and rare cold injury with prolonged or intense cooling.

name: High-frequency wand

angle.text: Skincare users run the wand over the face hoping to dry out pimples, tighten pores and improve skin clarity, and some promote it for anti-aging. It descends from early electrotherapy devices. Controlled evidence for these appearance uses is limited, and most support is anecdotal or from manufacturers.

summary: Purple lightning, weak evidence.
currentQuick:
A high-frequency wand is a handheld glass electrode that produces a low-current, high-voltage alternating current, giving a violet glow and ozone smell. It descends from the old Darsonval devices and is marketed for acne, pores and anti-aging.
It appears in skincare routines as a spot treatment, but the claims are largely unproven.
How it works: The current is said to generate ozone and mild heat that kill acne bacteria and boost circulation. Only laboratory evidence supports an antibacterial effect.
Risks and caveats: Risks include irritation and burns from misuse, and it is contraindicated with pacemakers or pregnancy. The only study found tested a similar device in vitro against skin bacteria, with no human trials located, so the claims are unproven. It has not been shown to substitute for established acne treatment.
deepLead:
A high-frequency wand is a handheld skincare device that passes a low-current, high-voltage, high-frequency alternating current through a gas-filled glass electrode held close to the skin, producing a violet glow and a faint ozone smell. It is marketed for acne, pores, congestion and anti-aging and descends from the electrotherapy devices of the late nineteenth century, often called d'Arsonval or violet-ray devices.
The best-known study of the technology is a 2022 laboratory experiment in which a commercial high-frequency device reduced colony counts of several skin bacteria, Cutibacterium acnes and dermatophyte fungi grown on agar plates. The authors called for studies in people to confirm any clinical effect. No randomized human trial of a consumer high-frequency wand for acne or skin appearance has been identified.
Manufacturers and skincare professionals typically list contraindications such as pacemakers and pregnancy, and misuse can cause irritation or burns.

name: Face slimming strap

chain: Slimmer-looking jaw and less double chin
angle.text: Sellers and users promote elastic chin straps to reduce the look of a double chin and sharpen the jawline. Similar straps are used medically to hold the mouth closed. Their lasting effect on facial fat or structure appears untested; any change is described as temporary compression.

summary: Compression does not melt fat or move bone. Full stop.
currentQuick:
A face slimming strap is an elastic band worn under the chin and over the head to compress the lower face and neck. It is marketed for reducing a double chin and defining the jawline.
It is mostly sold through social media and online marketplaces.
How it works: The strap presses on the skin and underlying tissue, which may briefly push fluid away or hold the jaw in position. It does not remove fat cells or change bone.
Risks and caveats: Risks are skin irritation, discomfort and unmet expectations, and tight wear could affect breathing or sleep. No clinical study of compression straps was found; reviews of submental fullness support injections, cryolipolysis and energy devices instead, while a jaw-exercise case report found no change. The closest evidence does not support the marketing claims.
deepLead:
A face slimming strap is an elastic band worn under the chin and over the head or ears to compress the lower face and neck. It is marketed for reducing the look of a double chin and defining the jawline and is sold mainly through online marketplaces and social media. Similar straps, called chin straps, are also used in medical settings, for example to keep the mouth closed during positive airway pressure therapy.
No published clinical study appears to have tested compression straps for slimming the face or reducing submental fat. Published reviews of non-surgical treatments for submental fullness cover injectable deoxycholic acid, cryolipolysis, radiofrequency, focused ultrasound and similar interventions, and do not mention compression straps. A small case report of a commercially sold jaw exerciser reported no change in jawline or double chin.
Proponents say that compression briefly pushes fluid away or holds the jaw in a tighter position; there is no evidence that the effect persists once the strap is removed.

name: Nose reshaping clip

chain: Clip presses on nose for hours
angle.text: Users wear silicone or plastic nose shapers hoping to lift the tip, narrow the bridge or straighten the nose without surgery. This is marketed as a non-surgical alternative to rhinoplasty. Evidence for lasting shape change in adults is lacking, with support resting on advertising and personal reports.

summary: Adult cartilage does not care about a clothespin.
currentQuick:
A nose reshaping clip is a soft plastic or silicone device that pinches the nose, often worn for hours, and is marketed as a way to lift the tip or narrow the bridge without surgery. Similar items are called nose shapers or lifters.
It appeals to people seeking rhinoplasty-like results at lower cost.
How it works: The clip applies external pressure to the cartilage and soft tissue. In infants, nasal molding can reshape soft cartilage, but adult cartilage and bone are rigid and do not change with sustained pressure.
Risks and caveats: Risks are skin irritation, pressure marks and breathing discomfort. No controlled trials of splints or clips for adult nasal shaping were found; the nearest evidence concerns nasal molding in infants and non-surgical filler rhinoplasty, which are different interventions. The claim is unsupported by published evidence, and cosmetic changes to the nose are normally assessed by a surgeon.
deepLead:
A nose reshaping clip, also sold as a nose shaper, lifter or slimmer, is a soft plastic or silicone device that is clipped or fitted onto the nose and worn for periods of time. It is marketed as a non-surgical way to lift the tip, narrow the bridge or straighten the nose.
No controlled trial of such clips for reshaping the adult nose has been identified. The nearest published research concerns two different interventions: nasal molding appliances used under clinical supervision in reconstructive settings, and non-surgical rhinoplasty with hyaluronic acid filler. Nose clips are also studied in medicine for unrelated purposes, such as compression to control nosebleeds and as laboratory breathing aids.
Proponents say sustained gentle pressure can retrain nasal cartilage over time; researchers have not tested this for commercial clips.

name: Facial lifting tape

chain: Tighter-looking face for photos or events
angle.text: Tape and invisible lifting patches are used, often hidden under hair, to pull cheeks and jawline taut for a temporary lifted look in photos, film and events. It is a styling trick with a long history in photography. It does not claim lasting change in skin.

summary: Physically pulls skin into place. Works exactly until you take it off.
currentQuick:
Facial lifting tape consists of adhesive strips or invisible patches placed on the cheeks, jawline or temples and pulled back, often hidden by hair, to temporarily smooth and lift sagging skin. It has been used in photography, TV and event styling for years.
The effect is cosmetic and immediate, and lasts only while the tape is on.
How it works: The adhesive physically holds skin in a tighter position, so the lift is mechanical, not biological. No change in collagen or tissue structure occurs.
Risks and caveats: Risks are skin irritation, adhesive allergy and redness on removal, and wearing it overnight can leave marks. Studies on facial tape concern post-surgical swelling and the mechanics of taped skin, not anti-aging, so the research does not support long-term claims. The effect is reliable but temporary.
deepLead:
Facial lifting tape consists of adhesive strips or invisible patches that are stuck to the cheeks, jawline or temples and pulled backward, usually hidden under hair or clothing, to temporarily tighten sagging skin. The practice has a long history in photography, film and event styling.
The lift is mechanical: the adhesive holds the skin in a different position while the tape is worn. No published study has examined whether lifting tape changes skin structure or produces any lasting effect, and the effect is expected to end when the tape is removed. Published research on facial taping concerns other uses, including elastic therapeutic tape for swelling after facial fracture surgery and taping as part of rehabilitation for Bell's palsy.
Reported drawbacks include skin irritation and adhesive reactions.

name: Lip plumping device

angle.text: Users apply suction cups to the lips as a do-it-yourself alternative to lip filler, aiming for a fuller look lasting a few hours. Suction pumps are listed among non-surgical lip augmentation options. The swelling is temporary, and evidence on safety and bruising comes mostly from case reports and user accounts.

summary: Suction swelling for a few hours. Bruising risk if you get greedy.
currentQuick:
A lip plumping device is a small cup or suction tool placed over the lips to draw blood and fluid into the tissue, producing a temporary swelling. Some versions add vibration or heat.
It is a do-it-yourself alternative to lip filler for a fuller look for a few hours.
How it works: Negative pressure pulls blood into the lip tissue and causes mild swelling and engorgement. No new tissue is created, so the effect fades quickly.
Risks and caveats: Too much suction can cause bruising, broken capillaries, pain or swelling, and results are short-lived. No peer-reviewed study of suction lip devices was found, only patents. The scholarly source listed concerns hyaluronic acid filler, which is a different intervention, and is included as the nearest research on lip enhancement safety.
deepLead:
A lip plumping device is a small cup or suction tool placed over the lips to draw blood and fluid into the tissue and produce temporary swelling. Some versions add vibration or warmth. It is promoted as a do-it-yourself alternative to lip filler that gives a fuller look for a short time. Wikipedia lists suction pumps among the non-surgical alternatives to lip augmentation, describing them as devices that use vacuum to raise pressure in the lips and cause temporary swelling.
No peer-reviewed clinical study of suction lip-plumping devices has been identified. Published research on lip plumping concerns topical plumper products, which act by irritation or vasodilation, and injectable fillers. Trials of topical plumpers have found short-lived increases in lip fullness lasting from minutes to a few hours, and case reports describe contact urticaria.
Reported risks of excessive suction include bruising, broken capillaries, pain and swelling; the effect is described as fading within hours.

name: Facial exerciser

chain: Fuller cheeks, defined jaw, less sagging
angle.text: Users hold silicone trainers in the mouth or against the cheeks, alongside facial yoga, hoping to build cheek and jaw muscle for a more defined, youthful face. The idea borrows from strength training elsewhere in the body. Evidence for aesthetic results is limited and mostly small or anecdotal.

summary: Cheek/smile trainers — weak evidence for any aesthetic outcome.
currentQuick:
Facial exercisers are small silicone or resistance devices placed in the mouth or on the cheeks to work the smile and cheek muscles, and are promoted alongside facial yoga routines. They are marketed for fuller cheeks, less sagging and a more youthful face.
The idea is to tone facial muscles the way gym training builds body muscle.
How it works: Repeated contraction against resistance may enlarge or strengthen the facial muscles, increasing cheek volume in the area they cover. Whether this meaningfully changes how the face looks is less clear.
Risks and caveats: Overuse can cause muscle soreness, jaw tension or temporomandibular strain, and repeated expressions may deepen some lines. Evidence is limited: the main study was a small uncontrolled trial of facial exercise in middle-aged women with high dropout and a conflict of interest, showing modest cheek fullness improvement. No trial tested the devices themselves.
deepLead:
Facial exercisers are small silicone or resistance devices held in the mouth or against the cheeks to work the smile, cheek and jaw muscles. They are sold alongside facial yoga routines and marketed for fuller cheeks, less sagging and a more youthful or more defined face. The underlying idea is that repeated contraction against resistance may strengthen or enlarge facial muscles, as strength training does elsewhere in the body.
No published trial has tested a commercial facial exerciser device for appearance. Research on facial exercise as a technique is limited: a 2014 systematic review found that all nine included studies reported positive outcomes but none used a control group or randomization, and concluded that the evidence was insufficient to judge effectiveness. A 2018 single-arm study of a 20-week facial exercise program in middle-aged women reported modest improvement in cheek fullness and estimated age. A 2024 case report of a jaw exerciser found no change in two users.
Facial exercise is also an established part of rehabilitation for facial palsy, which is a separate use.

name: Laser hair-growth cap

angle.text: Men and women with pattern hair loss wear light-emitting caps as a drug-free option, alone or alongside minoxidil or finasteride, to thicken hair and hold their hairline. Trials of FDA-cleared low-level light devices report density gains in androgenetic alopecia. Comparisons with drugs and add-on benefit are less established.

summary: FDA-cleared low-level light devices measurably improve density in pattern hair loss.
note: Per the AAD: helps, but won’t restore a full head of hair.
currentQuick:
A laser hair-growth cap is a wearable helmet-style device with an array of low-power red-light laser diodes or LEDs, worn for around 10 to 30 minutes on a set schedule. Several models hold US FDA clearance as devices for treating androgenetic alopecia, and they are sold as drug-free adjuncts to minoxidil or finasteride.
In looksmaxxing communities the caps are discussed as a hands-off way to slow or partly reverse thinning on the crown and hairline. The clinical literature reports a modest gain in hair density rather than full restoration, which is consistent with the dermatology-society position that the devices can help somewhat but do not return a full head of hair.
How it works: The approach is called low-level light therapy or photobiomodulation. Red light at roughly 650 nm is absorbed by chromophores in follicle cells, particularly in mitochondria, and is hypothesised to raise cellular energy output, prolong the growth phase of the hair cycle and reduce follicular inflammation. The exact pathway has not been established, and the optimal wavelength, dose and schedule have not been determined.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are reported as rare and mild, mostly scalp warmth, dryness or tingling. Pooled analyses of sham-controlled trials report an average density gain, but the trials are small, short and often manufacturer-linked, with substantial heterogeneity. Results are reported to depend on consistent use for months, and benefits fade when use stops. Many lower-priced caps sold online are LED-only products with no clinical data, so FDA clearance is specific to individual models. Studies and guidelines generally place the devices below finasteride or minoxidil in effect when used alone.
deepLead:
A laser hair-growth cap is a wearable helmet- or cap-style device containing an array of low-power red-light laser diodes or LEDs, worn for a set number of minutes on a regular schedule to treat thinning hair. It applies low-level laser (light) therapy, also called photobiomodulation, to the scalp and is sold as a drug-free option for androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss), alone or alongside minoxidil or finasteride.
Systematic reviews of randomized and clinical trials report that low-level laser therapy improved hair density in androgenetic alopecia compared with sham or baseline. A 2017 meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology found low-level laser therapy superior to placebo in men, with high heterogeneity among studies, and noted that the HairMax LaserComb is FDA-cleared for androgenetic alopecia. A 2016 systematic review of 11 studies (680 patients) found improved hair counts in nine, and a 2018 review of 13 trials reported significant improvement in 10 of 11 trials with statistical analysis.
The reviewers caution that studies are small and heterogeneous, optimal wavelengths and power are not established, and satisfaction gains were less marked than objective ones.
